title: Structural basis for the assembly and translocation of the Vip1-Vip2 insecticidal toxin from Bacillus thuringiensis

paper_content.abstract:
Insecticidal toxins from Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) have been extensively and successfully used in genetically
engineered crops for decades but continue to face challenges from the adaptive resistance in the insect population.
The Bt binary toxin Vip1Ad1(Vip1) and Vip2Ag1(Vip2), a promising next-generation candidate gene
combination for transgenic crops, have demonstrated high efficacy against the destructive coleopteran pest white
grubs, however, their mode of action remains largely elusive. In this study, we report cryo-EM structures of the
heptameric Vip1-pore and Vip2-bound Vip1-pore complex, capturing a series of putative assembly-related
intermediates that suggest a binary toxin assembly and translocation pathway. Together with structure-guided
mutagenesis, these data provide insights into a sequential assembly of binary complex and a sequence-
independent translocation mechanism. Proof-of-principle experiments showed successful delivery of a desired
protein cargo into host cells based on the mini-Vip2-Vip1 pore system, paving the way for developing much
needed extracellular pesticidal protein delivery platforms. These findings not only clarify the assembly and
translocation mechanism of the binary insecticidal toxin pair but also offer an excellent alternative model to
investigate human-pathogenic pore-forming toxin because of its similarity and biosafety.
paper_content.introduction:
Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is an entomopathogenic bacterium whose secreted toxins have been used as
biopesticides for pest control over several decades 1, such as the crystal proteins (Cry) family and the vegetative
insecticidal proteins (Vip) family 2-5. Most commercially deployed Bt toxins belong to the Cry family. However,
the increasing incidence of insect resistance to traditional Cry toxins has created an urgent need for alternative
pest control strategies 6. The Vip toxin family has been classified into four different subfamilies, namely Vip1,
Vip2, Vip3, and Vip4, based on their protein sequence similarity 7,8. Unlike the widely used single-component
Cry toxins, Vip1 and Vip2 act as binary toxins, with Vip2 exhibiting ADP-ribosyltransferase activity 9. The
nomenclature of Bt proteins generally consists of two components. The first denotes the protein’s type and
functional characteristics, while the second distinguishes different hierarchical ranks within that protein family.
These ranks follow a four-tier system-Arabic numerals, uppercase letters, lowercase letters, and a final set of
Arabic numerals-corresponding to sequence similarities of 45%, 78%, and 95% respectively 10. Vip1Ad1(Vip1)
and Vip2Ag1(Vip2) from Bt strain HBF-18 are members of the Vip1-Vip2 binary toxin translocation system,
and they can be effective against the notorious coleoptera insects Holotrichia parallela larvae that severely
damage many crops 11,12.

Binary toxins typically contain two components that are responsible for forming transmembrane pores and
inducing cytotoxicity, respectively. The pore-forming component can specifically recognize receptors on the
surface of host cells and forms a transmembrane pore that facilitate the translocation of toxin proteins into the
host cytosol 13,14. Binary toxin systems have been broadly used for infection by different human pathogens, such
as Clostridioides difficile CDT toxin (CDTa and CDTb) 15, Clostridium botulinum C2 toxin (C2I and C2II) 16,
Clostridium perfringens iota toxin (Ia and Ib) 17, Clostridium spiroforme CST toxin (CSTa and CSTb) 18, and
Bacillus anthracis anthrax toxin (PA, EF and LF) 19. In contrast to these human pathogens, Bt is widely used for
plant protection, providing significant benefits to agriculture worldwide.

As two of the few effective toxins, the Vip1-Vip2 binary toxins have shown significant potential in
controlling corn rootworm (e.g., Diabrotica virgifera) 6 and white grubs (e.g., Holotrichia parallela) 6, which
are major insect pests worldwide. These toxins are considered as strong candidates for second-generation
transgenic crops. However, two key unknowns have hindered their application. First, the molecular mechanism
underlying the functional assembly of the Vip1-Vip2 complex and its subsequent insecticidal actions on target
cells remains largely unclear, despite the elucidation of the crystal structures of Vip1 (PDB: 6SMS
[https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb6sms/pdb]) and Vip2 9. Second, while Vip2 prevents actin polymerization, which
makes its expression in planta lethal, some Vip2 mutants with reduced ADP-ribosyltransferase activity has been
engineered 20. Although previous studies have provided important insights, the lack of understanding of Vip2
translocation remains a major limitation of understanding and engineering Vip1-Vip2 system. Therefore,
elucidating the functional assembly mechanism of Vip1-Vip2 and the translocation mechanism of Vip2 is
essential for leveraging these toxins in the development of effective and targeted strategies for future
biotechnological applications.

Here, we determined the cryo-EM structures of the functional heptameric Vip1-pore and its complex with
Vip2, revealing that the heptameric β-barrel channel is highly hydrophilic which is crucial for sequence
independent Vip1 translocation. Additionally, we captured critical putative assembly-related intermediates
during the assembly of both the heptameric pore and the Vip2-bound Vip1-pore complexes, uncovering a putative
stepwise assembly mechanism. Moreover, through domain swapping of Vip2, we provided proof-of-concept
evidence for using N-terminal domain of Vip2 as a mini vector for protein translocation, which has high potential
for the translocation of other biopesticides. Together, these findings indicate the putative stepwise assembly and
sequence-independent translocation mechanism of the binary toxins and offer strategies for developing next-
generation biopesticides.
paper_content.results:
Overall structure of Vip1 heptameric pore
It is widely accepted that Bt Vip1 protoxin is digested by proteases in the midgut of targeting pest. The protease
digestion of Vip1 protoxin is indispensable for the pore formation that was assumed to deliver the enzymatic
Vip2 component into target cells2. We monitored the pore formation systematically by digesting Vip1 using
trypsin and obtained a stable oligomerization condition suitable for cryo-EM structure studies (Fig. 1a,
Supplementary Fig. 1a and 1c-f). In principle, the Vip1 protoxin was digested into a stable fragment within 2
hours under tested conditions, which further assembled into an SDS-resistant and heat-stable homogeneous
oligomer (Fig. 1b). We then determined the Vip1 oligomer at a resolution of 3.31 Å (Supplementary Table 1),
including data processing and representative density (Supplementary Fig. 2 and 3b). The structure of Vip1
oligomer adopted a stable heptamer manner (Fig. 1c-d), and the protomer of which is composed by four distinct
domains: D1 (D223-P305), D2 (S306-K512), D3 (T513-S622), and D4 (S623-F878) (Fig. 1e). It is worth noting
that the long stem of the pore structure, spanning residues K320 to F381, is encased by the D4 domain, which
comprises two sub-domains, D4I (S623-I756) and D4II (I769-F878), connected by a linker (S757-E768). The
D4 domain was reported as receptor-binding domain (RBD) in the B component of other binary toxins, such as
Ib and CDTb 21-23.

The Vip1 heptamer resembles a funnel shaped structure, termed Vip1-pore hereafter, with the upper part of
the open region containing four conserved motifs, which were involved in the recognition of enzyme components
in other binary toxin 22,24, and the lower part consisting of a cylindrical stem structure. In detail, the upper half
of the open region consists of four checkpoints. The first checkpoint, with an inner diameter of 36.2 Å, includes
seven di-calcium binding sites and was defined as Ca2+-edge. The second checkpoint, which is similar to the
NSS-loop in CDTb, is defined as the DTH-loop (residues D491-H493) in Vip1 (Fig. 1f-h). The narrowest
checkpoint formed by seven Phe residues (F455) from the heptamer, with an inner diameter of 6.0 Å, was defined
as ϕ-clamp 25. The fourth checkpoint locating at the top of the stem region has an inner diameter of 20.0 Å (Fig.
1h).

In the cylindrical stem, the pore forming region (K320-F381) of each protomer adopts an antiparallel β-
sheet structure and twists together to form the β-barrel stem, with a height of about 80.0 Å (Fig. 1d). A structural
comparison between the protomer and the predicted protoxin revealed drastic secondary structural differences
in the long stem region (Supplementary Fig. 4a-b). Strikingly, the secondary structure of the pore forming region
flipped nearly 180°, switching from a flexible loop to a rigid antiparallel β-sheet (Supplementary Fig. 4c). This
may have been triggered by the release of restriction by the N-terminal domain (D32-I222) of Vip1, which
provides the structural basis for the initiation of β-barrel pore formation.

Structure of Vip2-bound Vip1-pore heptamer complex
To explore the recognition and translocation mechanism of Vip2-Vip1 binary toxin, we established a pull-down
assay to monitor the interaction between Vip2 and Vip1 heptamer, which was also used for Vip2 and Vip1
heptamer complex assembly for cryo-EM studies (Fig. 2a-b and Supplementary Fig. 1b). We determined the
structure of Vip2 in complex with the Vip1 heptamer at a high resolution of 2.40 Å (Supplementary Table 1,
Supplementary Fig. 3c, 5 and 6), with Vip2 positioned within the wide opening of funnel-like Vip1 heptamer via
asymmetric interactions with four of the seven protomers (Fig. 2c-d). The total interaction area of Vip2-Vip1 is
about 1661.1 Å2 (Supplementary Table 2). In the complex, the overall structure of Vip1 heptamer is almost
identical to the Vip1-pore alone, with an RMSD of 0.862 Å. In short, Vip2 is a mixed α/β protein and could be
divided into two domains, an N-terminal Vip1 binding domain (residues A73-S265) and a C-terminal ADP-
ribosyltransferase domain (residues L266-T461), which is essential for actin modification (Fig. 2e) 9. The N-
terminal domain (NTD) of Vip2 is recognized by the upper part of the Vip1 heptamer funnel via extensive
interactions with the Ca2+-edge and DTH loop, whereas the C-terminal domain (CTD) remains largely
disengaged from the heptamer (Fig. 2f).

Vip2 is specifically recognized by the Vip1 heptamer mainly through subunit B, C, D, E via hydrogen bonds,
salt bridges, as well as hydrophobic interaction (Fig. 2g-k, and Supplementary Tables 2). In detail, K250 of Vip2
forms a hydrogen bond with T492 of the subunit B, while K251 interacts with E282, D287, and K490 of the
same subunit (Fig. 2h, and Supplementary Table 2). Right beside this, S232, I248, and Y281 of the subunit B
interact with the main-chain of the K251-F253 (KGF) loop of Vip2, which helps K251 of Vip2 to root in the
groove of the subunit B (Fig. 2g-h). Moreover, N163 of Vip2 interacts with S232 of the subunit B, which
stabilizes the conformation of the G162-T164 loop of Vip2 , further enhancing the interactions between Vip2 and
Vip1 (Fig. 2h). Meanwhile, the β-sheet of K244-E254 and the helix of I165-L178 of Vip2 forms extensive
interaction with the subunits C of Vip1 heptamer (Fig. 2i, and Supplementary Table 2). In detail, the K244,
K247 and V249 of Vip2 interact with the backbone of Ca2+-edge of the subunit C, and K174 of Vip2 interacts with
D225 in the Ca2+-edge of the subunit C (Fig. 2i).

Subunit D plays a crucial role in the recognition and translocation of Vip2. The N-terminal helix 1 (residues
A73-E83), N137-S139 loop, and S211-T216 loop of Vip2 participate in the interaction with the subunit D (Fig.
2j, and Supplementary Table 2). Additionally, Vip2 interacts with the DTH loop of subunit E via its T87-E90
loop (Fig. 2k). The N-terminal helix of Vip2 is nearly parallel to the main-chain of the subunit D from T498 to
E501 involving van der Waals interactions (Fig. 2l). Furthermore, W76 of Vip2 forms an interaction with the
DTH loop of the subunit D (Fig. 2l), and the on-going unfolded N-terminus of Vip2 is 17.7 Å away from the ϕ-
clamp checkpoint (Fig. 2l). We also observed an additional asymmetric density in the narrow checkpoint
surrounded by the ϕ-clamp in the complex structure of Vip2-Vip1 heptamer (Supplementary Fig. 7a-b). This
density should be part of the distal N-terminal region (residues N34-K72) of Vip2, indicating that the currently
obtained heptameric state of Vip1-Vip2 represents a putative translocation intermediate. Previous studies
revealed that deletion of the same region (α1-α3 helices, residues E27-Y59) of CDTa did not affect the binding
of toxin proteins, but the translocation efficiency decreased significantly, further supporting that the N-terminal
helix is essential for toxin protein translocation 23.

Compared with the structure of the other six subunits within the Vip1-Vip2 complex, the side-chain of H493
in subunit D undergoes a conformational shift upon complex formation and directly participates in Vip2 binding
(Supplementary Fig. 7c-e). This suggests that H493, located within the DTH loop of Vip1, may act as a switch
for the recognition of Vip2. The extensive interactions between Vip2 and Vip1 heptamer reveals structural basis
for the recognition of Vip2 by Vip1 heptamer.

Stepwise assembly of the Vip2-bound heptameric pore complex
The Vip1-Vip2 complex, as a binary toxin, has to be fully functional in the insect's midgut, where the toxins have
to be exposed to numerous proteases and endure fluctuating pH levels, particularly highly alkaline environment
26 , raising concerns about the stability of the complex. We challenged the stability of the pre-assembled Vip2-
bound Vip1 heptamer complex under a pH gradient and verified its integrity using a two-way rebinding assay,
which employs two distinct affinity tags on Vip2 or Vip1, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Using the Twin-strep tagged Vip2 for rebinding, we found that the binding ratios between Vip1 and Vip2
are comparable at pH ranging from 4.2 to 9.5 (Supplementary Fig. 8a). The clear off-ratio of the complex began
to emerge at pH 10.0, indicating either some artifacts or pH-induced disassembly of the complex. To further
explore these possibilities, we performed analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) at pH 10.4. In the absence of Vip2,
Vip1 alone exhibited multiple oligomeric species, consistent with partial pH-induced disassembly of the pore.
Notably, upon addition of Vip2, the sedimentation coefficients of Vip1 tetramers, pentamers, and heptamers
increased by 1.19%, 4.38%, and 11.83%, respectively, whereas no change was observed for Vip1 monomers
(Supplementary Fig. 9). These results indicate that Vip2 can associate with oligomeric forms of Vip1 and that
this interaction scales with oligomer size.

The appearance of off-ratio binding at high pH prompted us to investigate whether trace amounts of the
complex could survive at high pH, potentially adopting a conformation distinct from that observed at regular pH.
Motivated by the observed off-ratio results, in which an excess of Twin-Strep-tagged Vip2 was captured, we
intentionally reversed the affinity configuration to selectively isolate the trace amount of complex present at high
pH while eliminating the overwhelming excess of Vip1. Hence, we reversed the rebinding approach using Vip1
heptamer to bind to Ni resin under screened pH from 9.0 to 10.6 and found that the presence of Vip1-Vip2
complex at these harsh pH conditions (Supplementary Fig. 8b). This suggested the possible co-existence of the
Vip1-Vip2 complex and previously uncharacterized species at extremely alkaline environment 26, after
comparing the two-way rebinding assay.

To further characterize these species, we collected a full cryo-EM dataset about 8,961 movies at this pH
10.4. During 2D classification, we identified numerous putative assembly-related intermediates, corresponding
to Vip2-bound Vip1 heptamer complex, such as the two-subunit partial pore, the incomplete 1:3 (Vip2:Vip1)
complex, and the 1:4 to 1:7 complex (Fig. 3a). Because these species were observed under highly alkaline
conditions, we considered whether they might reflect pH-induced artifacts or disassembly products rather than
biologically relevant complexes. To address this concern, we performed chemical cross-linking experiments
under pH 7.5. As a control, pre-oligomerized Vip1 was crosslinked with comparable efficiency to the input,
showing no apparent accumulation of intermediate species (Supplementary Fig. 10a). In contrast, distinct pre-
assembly intermediate states were clearly captured by the crosslinking assay in the experimental group, in which
the crosslinker and trypsin were added simultaneously to the Vip1 protoxin (Supplementary Fig. 10b).
Furthermore, when Vip2 was present, combined cross-linking and Western blot analyses revealed Vip2-
associated complexes corresponding to several Vip1 binding intermediate states (Supplementary Fig. 11b).
Together, these observations support the existence of Vip1-Vip2 complexes involving distinct oligomeric forms
of Vip1 and suggest that the species identified by cryo-EM represent putative assembly-related intermediates,
rather than exclusively pH-induced disassembly products.

We then successfully reconstructed a low-resolution 3D map for an incomplete 1:4 (Vip2:Vip1) complex,
which matched the complete 1:7 (Vip2:Vip1) complex well, indicating that this 1:4 complex may represent a
putative intermediate state during complex assembly (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 12 and 13). Meanwhile, we
also solved a partial heptameric complex structure of 1:5 (Vip2:Vip1) complex at a resolution of 3.05 Å
(Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 3d and 13), which includes the Vip2 in complex with five Vip1
subunits, while missing two subunits for a complete heptamer (Fig. 3c-d).

The overall structure of Vip1 in the 1:5 complex closely resembles that of the Vip2 bound Vip1 heptamer
complex (RMSD = 0.569 Å) (Fig. 3e). Although most regions of Vip2 are highly identical between the two
complexes, the distal N-terminal helix 1 of Vip2 exhibits a pronounced conformational difference. Specifically,
when helix 2 of Vip2 is aligned between the 1:7 and 1:5 complexes, helix 1 shows an approximately 50° shift
(Fig. 3f-g). Furthermore, relative to the key ϕ-clamp residue F455 in Vip1, Vip2 appears to penetrate more deeply
into the heptamer in the 1:7 complex (Fig. 3e), which also differs from the configuration observed in CDTa and
Ia (Supplementary Fig. 14b-e). To our knowledge, this is the most in-depth intermediate complex structure of
homologous binary toxin in the translocation process (Supplementary Fig. 14b-e). In addition, the short loop
(residues K62-K70) and a 13 amino acids α-helix 1 (E71-E83) of Vip2 in the 1:5 complex structure shifted to a
disordered loop and an even shorter α-helix in the Vip2-bound heptamer complex structure, indicating that the
Vip2 conformations we captured here may represent an initial binding state as well as a pre-translocation state
(Fig. 3f-g). Notably, the overall structure of Vip2 in the 1:5 complex is highly consistent with that of the crystal
structure of Vip2 monomer (RMSD = 0.627 Å) (Supplementary Fig. 14a) 9, further supporting that this Vip2
conformation may represent an initial binding state for complex assembly.

In the 1:5 complex, the interface between Vip2 and Vip1 is strikingly different from that in the heptameric
structure, as only protomers B and C are involved in binding to Vip2 (Supplementary Fig. 14f). This indirectly
implies that subunits B and C of Vip1 are sufficient for initiating Vip2 recognition, while subunits D and E might
be essential for further translocation. Further 3D variability analysis (3DVA) of the 1:5 complex showed a
putative stepwise assembly process for the Vip2-bound Vip1 oligomers from the 1:5 complex to 1:6 complex
(Supplementary movie S1).

Dynamic translocation of Vip2 by the heptameric pore
As mentioned above, the distal N-terminal helix (A73-E83) of Vip2 in the heptameric complex has undergone
drastic secondary structure shift and significant conformational change (Fig. 3f-g). Remarkably, the K62-A73
region at the N-terminus of Vip2 in the Vip2-bound Vip1 pentamer complex is displayed as a loop connected to
the first helix, with E64 and E68 of Vip2 interact with the DTH loop of subunit C and B, respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 14g). In contrast, the same region is almost invisible when binding to the Vip1-pore in the
heptamer, indicating that the two structures may represent the initial binding and pre-translocation stages, with
unfolding of Vip2 occurring upon binding to the pore. Although there are significant differences in the
conformation of Vip2 in the two complex structures, the mode of interaction between Vip1 and KGF loop of
Vip2 is highly consistent (Fig. 3e), suggesting that the KGF loop is crucial for both recognition and translocation
of Vip2.

We were also able to reconstruct a 1:7 complex using the same dataset, which is highly similar to the
aforementioned Vip2-bound Vip1 heptamer complex under regular pH. The 3D variability analysis (3DVA) of
the 1:7 complex displayed the dynamic translocation of Vip2 by the heptamer (Supplementary movie S2). Firstly,
Vip2 binds to the pore of the Vip1 heptamer via specific interactions between the KGF loop of Vip2 and the
Ca2+-edge and DTH loop of B subunit of the Vip1 heptamer (Fig. 3h). Then, the N-terminal helix of Vip2 binds
to the DTH loop, preparing for the translocation of Vip2 (Fig. 3i). Subsequently, Vip2 rotates inward toward the
pore of the Vip1 heptamer, anchoring via the KGF loop (Fig. 3e). Concurrently, as Vip2 rotates and the DTH
loop is extruded, its N-terminal helical structure unfolds and begins to penetrate the pore in the form of a linear
peptide chain. Once the Vip2 peptide chain passes through the constriction formed by F455, it is further
translocated into the β-barrel channel (Fig. 3j). Together with the 3DVA, the successful capture of the putative
assembly-related intermediates provides a delicate scenario for the assembly and dynamic translocation of the
binary toxin (Fig. 3h-j).

Translocation of the binary toxin is hydrophilicity dependent and sequence independent
Vip1 adopts a classical heptameric β-barrel structure, which is similar to those of CDTb, Ib and anthrax toxin
PA 24,27. Surprisingly, 96% of residues in the interior of Vip1-pore are hydrophilic and 4% of them are
hydrophobic (Fig. 4a). However, in the predicted protoxin structure, the stem region of Vip1 is generally
composed of an amphipathic flexible loop, containing 69.4% of hydrophilic and 30.6% of hydrophobic residues.
These hydrophilic residues converged at the inner pore portion, providing a highly hydrophilic pore (Fig. 4a).

The highly hydrophilic pore is supported by other binary toxins, as revealed by structural comparison combined
with sequence analysis of the stem region. In addition, 72.4% of the residues lining in the inner tunnel of Vip1
heptamer are small side-chain and hydrophilic amino acids, such as Ser, Thr and Gly (Fig. 4b). 13.8% of the
residues on the inner surface of the Vip1-pore are charged residues, including E327, H329, E370, and E360 (Fig.
4a), and only one hydrophobic residue A368 could be observed. The highly hydrophilic residue preference of
the pore intrigues us to ask whether it is essential for the translocation of unfolded Vip2 peptide across the pore,
as all the enzymatic proteins in binary toxins have to be unfolded for translocation 28.

To explore the influence of hydrophilic residues on the translocation of Vip2, structure-based mutagenesis
on key residues inside the pore of Vip1 were generated and further evaluated by insecticidal assay. We first
generated a hydrophilic mutant AT368S, which retained similar insecticidal activity to the WT, suggesting that
the hydrophobic residue is not essential for translocation (Fig. 4c). Next, three charged residues on the stem were
mutated to serine, generating E327S/H329S double mutant and E370S single mutant. E327S/H329S and E370S
did not display significant effects on insecticidal activity, indicating that charged residues might be dispensable
and hydrophilic serine replacement could be tolerated by Vip2 for translocation. Similarly, the reverse charge
mutant H329E showed minor effects on insecticidal activity, which might be caused by its large side-chain that
delayed the translocation efficiency (Fig. 4c). Reversely, two hydrophobic variants E327A/H329A as well as
E370V demonstrated minor decrease in insecticidal activity. We then combined the two variants and generated
an E327A/H329A/E370V triple mutant, which showed significant decrease in insecticidal activity. In contrast,
an E327S/H329S/E370S triple mutant still maintained high insecticidal activity, supporting that the sequence-
independent hydrophilic environment in the pore is critical for translocation (Fig. 4c). The folding of all mutants
was comparable with that of the wild type as shown in the thermal shift assays as well as the trypsin digestion
induced oligomerization assay (Supplementary Fig. 15). Consistently, hydrophobic variants caused dramatic
effects on ion selectivity, and changes in single-channel conductance were observed in Clostridium perfringens
iota toxin 29.

In order to verify the physiological relevance of the hydrophilic residues in the Vip1-pore regarding Vip2
translocation, histopathological staining on the larvae of H.parallela were analyzed. The histopathological
staining demonstrated that Vip1 combined with Vip2 toxins were able to cause substantial damage on the gut of
the larvae, including destruction of tissue structure and shedding of cellular content into the gut lumen (Fig. 4d).
In contrast, Vip1-E327A/H329A/E370V variant and Vip2 caused only slight damage to the gut, characterized by
loss of microvilli and intracellular vacuolation, while the tissue structure remained largely intact (Fig. 4e). As a
negative control, the gut treated with saline alone showed clear microvilli and intact gut cells (Fig. 4f). The
destruction of these tissues was further assessed, revealing that the damage caused by Vip1 and Vip2 toxins are
significantly higher than that in the saline-treated control group. In contrast, the Vip1-E327A/H329A/E370V
variant was less severe than the damage induced by Vip1 and Vip2 toxins (Fig. 4g). The insecticidal activity of
the triple hydrophobic variant significantly decreased, supporting the hydrophilic environment within the pore
is critical for the translocation and efficacy of Vip1-Vip2 binary toxin (Fig. 4c). Taken together, structural
analysis combined with mutagenesis data revealed that translocation of Vip2 is highly dependent on
hydrophilicity and sequence independent.

The hydrophilic pore of Vip1 has the potential for desired protein delivery
The sequence-independent and hydrophilicity-dependent translocation mechanism adopted by the Vip1-Vip2
complex prompted us to investigate whether it could be exploited for non-specific cargo delivery. To explore
this possibility, we established an assay to test the delivery capacity of the complex. We constructed a fusion
protein by attaching green fluorescent protein (GFP) to the C-terminus of full length Vip2, herein referred to as
Vip2-GFP, to assess whether it could be translocated into target cells (Fig. 5a). As shown in Figure 5b, after 3h
of incubation, successful translocation of Vip2-GFP into H.parallela HP9-2 cells could be observed by
subcellular localization assay. In contrast, the Vip1 loss-of-function triple mutant (E327A/H329A/E370V) failed
to translocate Vip2-GFP into cells, which is similar to the control group (Fig. 5b-c). This result supports the
notion that the Vip1-mediated translocation is sequence-independent, as otherwise the GFP domain might have
impeded translocation. Moreover, given that Vip2 could be divided into two functional domains, NTD which
mediates binding to Vip1, and CTD which exerts toxic activity, we next asked whether the NTD alone is
sufficient to drive translocation. To address this, we generated a second fusing protein Vip2NTD-GFP by replacing
the whole CTD of Vip2 with a GFP tag (Fig. 5a). Remarkably, the mini Vip2NTD-GFP was translocated with even
better efficiency into the H.parallela HP9-2 cell, as revealed by the subcellular localization assay (Fig. 5d-e).
These results further support the idea that translocation through the Vip1-pore is independent of the specific
sequence of the cargo.

Taken together, our findings provide comprehensive insights into the putative assembly and sequence-
independent translocation mechanism of binary complex, which may serve as a promising platform for non-
specific delivery of other target proteins (Fig. 6). In brief, Vip1 is proteolytically activated by host proteases to
form a pore structure (Vip1-pore). The fusion of a target protein with mini Vip2NTD, which acts as a guidance
module, enables specifical interaction with the Vip1-pore, thereby facilitating translocation across the cell
membrane. Upon entry into the cytosol, the fusion protein is likely assisted by molecular chaperones such as
Hsp70 and Hsp90 30-32, which promote proper refolding and functional recovery.

The successful delivery of a non-specific sequence not only supports our vision that Vip2 translocation is
sequence-independent, but also provides a molecular tool for future insecticidal drug development and delivery.
Vip2NTD-GFP displayed higher efficiency in the subcellular localization assay demonstrating that the NTD of
Vip2 could serve as a promising transport carrier for other protein biopesticides, which has high potential for the
next-generation drug development against rigorous drug resistance.
paper_content.methods:
Cloning, expression and purification of recombinant proteins
The full-length Vip1 (GenBank ID: AGC08395.1) and Vip2 (GenBank ID: AGC08396.1) proteins were natively
expressed in Bt and purified via multi-step chromatographic purification 33. Briefly, Bt Vip1 and Vip2 were
cultured in LB at 30℃ for 24 h. The natively expressed and secreted Vip1 and Vip2 were purified using ion
exchange chromatography. Prior to loading, each sample was diluted 10-fold by buffer A (25 mM Tris-HCl, pH
8.0, 40 mM NaCl). Vip1 was purified using a HiTrap Q HP column, while Vip2 was purified on a HiTrap SP HP
column. Both columns were pre-equilibrated with buffer C and eluted with a linear gradient of buffer B (25 mM
Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl), increasing from 0% to 100 % Buffer B over 75 minutes. Then, the sample was
loaded onto a Superdex 200 Increase column (Cytiva, Marlborough, USA) and eluted with a buffer C (25 mM
Tris, pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl). The purity of the eluted fractions was subsequently assessed by SDS-PAGE.

The Vip1 protein with C-terminal His6-tag was cloned into pET-28a vector (Supplementary Table 3) and
further overexpressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) for pull-down assay and insecticidal bioassay. All mutants were
generated by overlapping PCR and further verified by DNA sequencing, with primers listed in Supplementary
Table 4. Vip2 (E41-K462) with C-terminal His-tag and N-terminal Twin-Strep tag was cloned into pET-28a and
overexpressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3). Bacteria were cultured in LB medium containing 100 μg/mL kanamycin.
Expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG (isopropyl 1-thio-β-d-galactopyranoside) when OD reached 0.6-
0.8, followed by culturing at 18°C for 18 h and harvested by centrifugation.

The harvested cells were lysed by sonication in lysis buffer D (50 mM Tris, pH 8.5, 400 mM NaCl),
followed by centrifugation at 30,624×g for 30 min. The supernatant containing soluble Vip1 or Vip2 protein was
loaded onto a Ni-NTA column pre-equilibrated with lysis buffer D. Vip1 or Vip2 protein was eluted using buffer
E (50 mM Tris, pH 8.5, 400 mM NaCl, 300 mM imidazole). Further purification of the recombinant Vip1 and
Vip2 proteins was performed similarly to that of the native tagless Vip1 and Vip2, respectively 33 .

Assembly of Vip1 heptameric pore and Vip1-Vip2 complex
To establish conditions that promote Vip1 oligomerization, the effects of trypsin concentration and digestion
duration were systematically evaluated. A series of controlled proteolytic digestions was performed at 37℃ using
varying trypsin concentrations (Trypsin:Vip1 mass ratios ranging from 1:10 to 1:100), digestion times (0.5-60
h), ethanol concentrations (0-20%), and different oligomerization times (0-36 h). The results show that a mass
ratio of 1:100 (Trypsin:Vip1) at 37°C for 2 h is sufficient to achieve homogeneous activation of Vip1. The
digestion reactions were subsequently quenched by the addition of 2 mM PMSF to inhibit further proteolysis
and allow Vip1 self-assembly to proceed.

The tagless Vip2 was mixed with Vip1 oligomer at a molar ratio of 3:1 (Vip2:Vip1 oligomer) and incubated
at 8 °C for 12 h. The Vip1-Vip2 complex was further purified by Ni-NTA column, as we serendipitously found
that the oligomeric pore could bind to Ni-NTA resin, which is probably due to multiple adjacent histidine residues.
The complex was then buffer-exchanged into a solution containing 25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and 100 mM NaCl
for cryo-EM sample preparation.

Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection
The trypsin-activated Vip1 heptamer was applied to glow-discharged carbon-coated copper grids (300 mesh,
QUANTIFOIL® R 1.2/1.3) at a final concentration of 1.5 mg/mL. The grids were blotted and plunge-frozen in
liquid ethane using an FEI Vitrobot-MarkI (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rockford, USA). The frozen grids were
screened and then transferred to a Glacios 200kV TEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rockford, USA) equipped
with a Falcon 4 direct electron detector for data acquisition. Cryo-EM images were automatically collected using
a defocus range of -1 to -2 μm, a nominal magnification of 150,000×, a calibrated pixel size of 0.94 Å/pixel. An
exposure time of 5.52 s was employed at an electron dose rate of 9.05 e⁻/Å²/s.

The two Vip1-Vip2 complexes were applied to the glow-discharged Quantifoil R1.2/1.3 grids at a final
concentration of 1.5 mg/mL and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen using the same Vitrobot.
The screened frozen grids were then transferred to a 300kV cryo-electron microscope (Titan Krios G4, Thermo
Fisher Scientific, Rockford, USA) equipped with a Gatan K3 electron detector and a GIF BioQuantum energy
filter for data acquisition. Images were collected on a Titan Krios microscope using a defocus range of -1 to -
2 μm, a nominal magnification of 105,000×, and a binned pixel size of 0.84 Å/pixel. Energy filtering was
performed with a slit width of 20 eV. An exposure time of 2.16 s was employed at an electron dose rate of
23.148 e⁻/Å²/s. Micrographs were recorded as movie stacks consisting of 40 frames, with a total electron dose
of 50 e⁻/Å² and an electron fluence of 1.25 e⁻/Å² per frame. All data collection was automated using EPU
software.

Cryo-EM data processing
Patch motion correction and contrast transfer function (CTF) estimation were performed for all acquired using
the patch CTF estimation module in cryoSPARC v4.0. For the Vip1-pore, a total of about 0.2 million particles
were automatically picked using Blob picker. Among these, 74,122 particles corresponding to heptamers with
high-resolution features were selected for further ab-initio reconstruction and heterogeneous refinement. A
predominant class containing 59,851 particles were selected for further refinement, resulting in a heptamer map
at an overall resolution of 3.31 Å with C7 symmetry.

Data processing of the Vip2-bound Vip1-pore complex followed the same procedure as above. Similarly,
particles were automatically picked using Blob picker, and around 3.2 million particles were selected for 2D
classification. A class representing the heptamer complex, containing 265,183 particles, was selected for
homogeneous refinement and NU-refinement with C1 symmetry, yielding a final map of 2.40 Å resolution.

Processing of the 1:4 and 1:5 (Vip2:Vip1) complex followed a similar workflow using the dataset collected
under pH 10.4. Approximately 4.5 million particles automatically picked using Blob picker and subjected to 2D
classification. The well-defined class representing for each complex were selected for ab-initio reconstruction,
followed by homogeneous refinement and NU-refinement with C1 symmetry.

Three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA) was performed in cryoSPARC. The analysis was conducted
using the final particle stack obtained from the consensus refinement. The soft mask generated during the
consensus refinement was directly used for the 3DVA calculation. Three variability modes were calculated to
visualize conformational heterogeneity. No particle subset selection, clustering, or further refinement was
performed following the 3DVA analysis. The resulting volumes were exported to generate the two supplementary
movies, respectively.

Model building and refinement
Model building of the four structures was accomplished in an iterative process involving SWISS-MODEL 51,
Coot 52, Chimera 53, and PHENIX 54. Briefly, for the structure determination of the 3.31 Å resolution heptameric
pore, the transmembrane antiparallel β-sheet of CDTb (PDB: 7YVQ [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb7yvq/pdb]) and
a model generated by SWISS-MODEL server were modified and used as an initial model for manually fitting to
the heptameric density map. Together with iterative manual building in Coot and real space refinement in Phenix,
the final heptameric structure was generated by applying the C7 symmetry and further refined in PHENIX.
Notably, the D4-II domain (S763-F878) was excluded in the Vip1-pore due to weak map density.

Using the structures of Vip1-pore and Vip2 (PDB: 1QS1 [https://doi.org/10.2210/pdb1qs1/pdb]) as input
models, we were able to generate an initial model for the Vip2-bound Vip1 heptamer complex using Chimera.
This initial structure model was used for iterative manual building in Coot and real space refinement in Phenix.
The N-terminal region (N34-K72 residues) of Vip2 was omitted due to weak density which might indicate high
flexibility. The model of partial D4-II domain (P783-F878) was excluded because of weak map density. The
model of the Vip2-bound Vip1 pentamer complex was built similarly as above. Briefly, the partial Vip1-pore
structure and Vip2 monomer were applied to fitting into the density map using Chimera.

Protein melting assay
The thermal stability of Vip1 variants was assessed using a fluorescence-based thermal shift assay performed on
a Real-Time PCR system. Each protein, at a concentration of approximately 0.5 mg/mL, was mixed with the
fluorescent dye SYPRO Orange (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, USA) and subjected to heating from 25°C to 95°C
with a linear temperature ramp. The melting midpoint (Tm) of each protein was determined using the analysis
software provided by the instrument manufacturer. The data from three independent experiments were averaged
to generate the bar graph.

Insect and cell line
The larva of Holotrichia parallela were obtained from the field of peanut supplied by Cangzhou Academy of
Agriculture and Forestry Sciences. HP9-2, an established cell line derived from embryonic cell of H.parallela
was obtained as a seed culture from Qingdao Agricultural University, and grown at Institute of Plant Protection
in Trichoplusia ni Medium-Formulation Hink (TNM-FH) insect cell culture medium (Pricella, Wuhan, China)
55 supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (VivaCell Biosciences, Shanghai, China). The cells were
grown at 28°C in 25 cm2 tissue culture flasks and transferred to fresh medium every 5-7 days.

Insecticidal bioassay
Second instar larvae of H.parallela were starved for 12 h. Vip1 or its mutant proteins was mixed with Vip2 or
its mutant proteins with molar mass ratio 1:1 in 20 μL buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl containing 100 mM NaCl).
Twenty microgram mixed proteins were injected into larvae through their mouthparts. The buffer without protein
was treated as a negative control. Twelve larvae were injected for each treatment. Three repeats were performed.
The larvae were fed in soil mixed with shredded carrot at 26°C in artificial climate box. The mortality of larvae
was checked after 7 days. Corrected mortality was calculated by subtracting the mortality of the negative control
group from the mortality of each treatment group. Each assay was repeated at least three times 56.

Histopathological analyses
Six second-instar larvae of H. parallela were starved for 6 h for each treatment. Twenty microgram Vip1 or its
mutants and Vip2 proteins were injected into larvae through their mouthparts. The buffer without protein was
treated as a negative control. The larvae were fed in soil mixed with shredded carrot for 48 h at 26°C in artificial
climate box. The midgut tissues were dissected from these larvae and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Solarbio
Life Sciences, Beijing, China) at 4°C overnight. The tissues were embedded in paraffin and made 5 µm thick
sections. The sections were stained with hematoxylin solution for 10 min and eosin solution for 30 s by using
Hematoxylin-Eosin (HE) Stain Kit according to manufacturer’s instructions (Solarbio Life Sciences, Beijing,
China), and sealed with neutral gum. The pathological changes in midgut tissues were observed under
Pannoramic 250 Flash digital microscopes (3DHISTECH, Budapest, Hungary). To further examine the damage
to tissues, we carried out histological analysis with paraffin embedded midgut tissue sections. These tissues were
scored according to four histological criteria including disruption of the epithelial microvilli, disorder of cell
arrangement, cell shedding, and cytoplasmic vacuolation on a scale of 0 to 3 (normal, mild, moderate, or severe).

Glutaraldehyde cross-linking
Purified Vip1 and Vip2 were buffer-exchanged into 20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, 100 mM NaCl using a Superdex
200 Increase column (Cytiva, Marlborough, USA). To assess Vip1 oligomerization, in the first group, purified
Vip1 was proteolytically activated by trypsin digestion and then pre-incubated for 12 hours to allow oligomer
formation. In the second group, trypsin-activated Vip1 was used without extended incubation, and
glutaraldehyde was added immediately after proteolytic activation. Both sets of samples were treated with
increasing concentrations of glutaraldehyde at 37°C for 2 h, followed by quenching with 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0).
The reactions were resolved by SDS-PAGE and visualized by Coomassie staining. In addition, eluted Vip1 was
mixed with Vip2 at molar ratios of 3:0, 3:1 or 3:3, followed by addition of trypsin and 2.5 mM CaCl₂.
Glutaraldehyde was then added to 0.0075% (w/v), and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 2 h. All reactions
were quenched with Tris (pH 8.0, final 0.1 M) for 20 min. Samples were resolved by SDS-PAGE and visualized
by Coomassie staining.

Western blotting
For western blotting analysis, samples were separated by Young PAGE™ 4-20% Bis-Tris (GenScript, Piscataway,
USA). Proteins were transferred onto 0.45 μm PVDF membrane (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) in Tris-Glycine
transfer buffer (25mM Tris, 200mM Glycine). Membranes were blocked in 5% milk in TBS-T for 1 h prior to
incubation with StrepII Tag mouse monoclonal antibody (AF2924, 1:1,500 dilution, Beyotime, Shanghai, China)
overnight. The following day, membranes were incubated with HRP-labeled Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H+L)
(A0216, 1:1,500 dilution, Beyotime, Shanghai, China) in TBS-T and visualized using ECL Prime reagent
(Beyotime, Shanghai, China).

Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC)
Sedimentation velocity experiments were carried out at 20℃ and 90,000×g on a Beckman Coulter Optima AUC
following standard protocols 57. Samples containing either 1 mg/mL Vip1 alone or 1 mg/mL Vip1 pre-mixed
with Vip2 at a 1:3 mole ratio were prepared in buffer (50 mM CAPS, 100 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM CaCl₂, pH 10.4).
The mixtures were then treated with trypsin at a Vip1:trypsin mass ratio of 100:1 and incubated at 37°C for 2 h
before being loaded into 12-mm Epon centerpieces for analytical ultracentrifugation. Absorbance (280 nm) and
interference scans were collected at 60 s intervals. Data analysis was performed with SEDFIT (Version 18p1)
using a Continuous c(s) Distribution model as described by Schuck et al. 58.

Observation of subcellular localization
H.parallela HP9-2 cells were suspended at 1×10⁷ cells/mL in TNM-FH insect cell culture medium supplemented
with 10% FBS, and 500 μL aliquots were transferred to glass bottom cell culture dishes (801001, NEST, Wuxi,
China). The dishes were incubated at 28°C overnight. Four hundred microliters TNM-FH culture medium were
eliminated. One hundred microliters of 2000 nM Vip1, mixed with Vip2-GFP or Vip2NTD-GFP proteins were
added to the cells and the dishes incubated for 2 h at 28°C. Vip2-GFP or Vip2NTD-GFP protein with same amount
was added solely to the cells as negative control. One hundred microliters of 5000 nM Vip1, mixed with Vip2-
GFP or Vip2NTD-GFP proteins were added to the cells and the dishes incubated for 1.5 h or 3.5 h at 28°C. Cells
were washed twice with pH 7.4 PBS (Phosphate Buffer Saline) and fixed in 200 μL 4% paraformaldehyde for
30 min at room temperature. After washed three times with PBS, they were carefully permeabilized with 2%
Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 min at room temperature. After washing with PBS for 3 times, the cells were labeled
with 1×Phalloidin-iFluor 594 (Abcam, Cambridge, UK) for 1 h and 1×Hoechst33342 (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
Rockford, USA) for 10 min at room temperature. After washing with PBS for 3 times, Prolong Diamond
Antifade (Invitrogen, Oregon, USA) was added into the dishes. Images were obtained using confocal LSM 980
microscopes (Zeiss, Germany) 59.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Groups of Jie Zhang and Peng Chen present a structural and functional study of the Vip1-Vip2 toxin complex from Bacillus
thuringiensis. In the manuscript, I see the following three major messages:
I) The study reports a structure of the Vip1 heptamer and a structure of the Vip1-Vip2 complex, showing their similarity to
other binary proteins.
II) Following alkaline pH treatment, the researchers show the presence of Vip1-Vip2 complexes with different stoichiometry,
suggesting that they represent "critical intermediates".
III) The researchers demonstrate that Vip1-Vip2 complex can be used for translocation of the desired protein cargos.
As I have major concerns to all three messages, either in terms of methodological approaches, or in terms of novelty, I do not
recommend this paper for publishing.
Major points:
Message I.
1. In line 87, the authors write that 'it is widely accepted that Bt Vip1 prototoxin is digested...'. I find such statement without a
proper citation non appropriate for scientific literature. Please provide a reference.
2. In line 89 the authors report that they 'systematically monitored pore formation' with a reference to Fig 1a. However, I don't
see any systematic analysis there. What was it? How did the authors perform it? In Fig 1b the authors show an SDS-PAGE
suggesting that a high molecular weight band is the pore. It is quite an overstatement.
3. In line 105 the authors describe a region of Vip1 that is essential for the Vip2 translocation. How can it be deduced only
from the structure of Vip1?
4. Line 107. The authors built many metal ion binding sites. Indeed, they are of a good quality in cryo-EM maps, however,
what is the basis for being sure that it is calcium, and not, for example, magnesium?
5. The authors applied C7 symmetry for the Vip1 structure. What was the rationale for doing this? Could it be that the protein
has a pseudosymmetry that was lost when applying C7? Later, the authors compare Vip1 alone (refined with C7) and when
it complex with Vip2 (C1), is such a comparison justified?
I inspected the final cryo-EM maps and the structures and found them of a good fit. I appreciate that the authors voluntarily
provided them with the submission. However, after reading supplementary information, PDB reports and materials and
methods, I am raising the following concerns:
6. The cryo-EM reconstructions are of good resolution, however clashscores of the deposited structures are surprisingly bad.
For 9VEK is it 9 and for 9VEG is it 12. Considering this and the following points, I believe that authors need to revisit the
model building.
7. 9VEK contains 6 side chain outliers. It is fine having them, however the structure has 7 chains built into C7-symmetry
cryo-EM density. How is it possible to have 6 outliers?
8. All three structures contain bong angle outliers. Are they supported by the density?
9. Supplementary table 1 reports 'model resolution'. What is it? How is it different to 'map resolution' the authors provide
above other than it is given at different FSC threshold?
10. Please provide data on what residues have been built into the density, as the structures do not cover complete protein
sequences.
11. Supplementary figure 1, 3 and 5 are missing exemplary cryo-EM micrographs and 2D class averages.
12. Finally, it looks to me that the obtained structures are very similar to other binary toxins, like C2, Iota and others. What is
the new information gained from the Vip1-Vip2 complex?
Message 2.
13. In line 173 the authors mention 'two-way rebinding assay' but do not describe it. Could it be that at extreme pHs the
proteins do not bind to strep sepharose? I think this experiment misses a control.
14. While I find it interesting that at high pH the authors found the Vip1-Vip2 complex at different stoichiometry, I do not think
that based on that, one can claim that these are 'intermediate states' and deduce an assembly process (line 213). It all might
be artifacts of high pH or rather 'disassembly process'. I believe that functional assays are required to show that 5:1 Vip1-
Vip2 complex is a true intermediate and can be assembled further.
15. Line 223. The same as above. It is possible that high pH created nonphysiological artifacts that the authors interpreted
as intermediate states.
16. Fig 3a misses scale bars. I have my doubts that the 2D class on the very left represents a single Vip1. The class is of low
quality and can just contain some debris. I suggest reextracting these particles with lower box size and redoing 2D
classification to get some high-resolution features to prove that it is really a single Vip1.
Message 3.
17. While I find this interesting and a well-done set of experiments, I am questioning the novelty of them. For example,
Bacillus anthracis PA is used for decades for similar purpose. A few recent articles describing it:
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40758882/ https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25250705/
Minor points:
1. Abstract line 31. I would not use 'irrelevant' protein cargo but maybe non-specific, engineered or desired?
2. Introduction has several strange sentences that I could not follow. For example, first you describe 4 families of Vip proteins
(line 47) and, right after it, on line 50, talk about the Vip1-Vip2 family. Why?
3. What means Ad1 in Vip1Ad1 in line 49?
4. What is a pore-forming protein in line 54?
5. Anthrax toxin has two payloads, EF and LF. Why only to mention the second?
6. Line 71-72: the authors state that the lack of the Vip2 translocation mechanism is a major limitation... of what? I couldn't
follow. Of engineering of Vip2 to be nontoxic to plants?
7. Line 87-88. 'which is indispensable for the pore formation'. Is it the pest, which is indispensable?
8. Line 101, what homologous protein you have in mind?
9. Line 192 cites Supplementary Fig 5a-e, while it is cryo-EM supplementary figure.
10. Line 397. Please describe the method of purification of Vip1 in detail.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript presents novel cryo-EM structures formed by insecticidal toxins from Bacillus thuringiensis.
1. The high resolution structures of Vip1 heptameric pore and Vip2-bound Vip1-pore heptamer complex are well described
and analysed and provide a valuable new structural information that supports a sequence-independent translocation
mechanism of the binary toxins. The findings will be a helpful addition to the field. To evaluate the quality of these structures
the reviewer requests access to cryo-EM maps including non-symmetrised maps, maps without masking and masks applied
prior to CTF estimation. We remind the authors that EMDB now encourages and accepts deposition of these together with
‘main’ structure. In addition, we will appreciate up-to-date PDB validation reports for all structures. Representative cryo-EM
images and averages of common views of Vip1 pore and Vip2/Vip1- complex should be also added to supplementary
information to aid understanding and evaluation of data presented.
While data analysis and image processing steps are well described in Methods section, some important information is
missing: please add which detector was used for data collection on Glacios instrument (Vip1 data), correct Vitrobot model
and replace ‘flash frozen’ ‘plunge frozen’ for cryo-Em grids. In addition, information about electron flux (e/A2/s), exposure
time (s) and electron fluence per frame (e/A2) should be added for each solved structure in Methods and/or in Table 1.
To put new structural information in context and show the significance to the field, Vip1 and Vip2/Vip1 structures should be
accompanied by analysis of sequence homology with other bacterial toxins: α-hemolysin, anthrax protective antigen pore,
Clostridium perfringens iota toxin and Vibrio cholerae cytolysin and comparison with known structures of membrane-inserted
pores of binary toxins.
While discussing translocation mechanism, we also suggest including speculations on driving forces for substrate protein
translocation: differences of proton concentration or electrical potential across the ϕ-clamp. The former requires protonation-
dependent conformational changes of two or more alternating gates and protonation-dependent conformational change in ϕ-
clamp region. Alternatively, translocation could follow charge-state dependent Brownian ratchet model similar to the one
described for anthrax protective antigen pore. Electrophysiological studies – if possible – would be a valuable addition.
2. Authors also described multiple incomplete assemblies of Vip2-bound Vip-pore heptamer complex after treatment with
high pH (pH 10.4): two-subunit partial pore,1:3 (Vip2:Vip1) complex, 1:4 and 1:7 complex. Low-resolution cryo-EM 3D
reconstructions of an incomplete 1:4 (Vip2:Vip1) complex and complete 1:7 (Vip2:Vip1) complex were obtained from this
preparation and discussed as intermediate states of complex assembly. This interpretation is only supported by fluctuating
pH levels in insect’s midgut, including highly alkaline environment. The authors did express some ‘concerns about
physiological relevance’ of these findings in Discussion section but nonetheless propose a step-wise assembly pathway
based on these ‘intermediate’ structures. No high pH treatment step was performed for Vip2/Vip1 preparation used for high
resolution structures discussed earlier, neither for subcellular localization experiments with insect cells reported in this
manuscript. To enable mechanistic understanding of Vip1/Vip1 complex formation and action, further in vitro experiments
are required using model liposomes and Vip2/Vip1 (or Vip2-GFP/Vip1): Vip2/Vip1 assemblies on liposomes could be
treated with high pH and then used for cryo-EM sample preparation. Image processing of these cryo-EM data would follow
already established single particle workflow using cryoSPARC and could yield direct visualisation of intermediate
structures. These experiments could also shed some light on nature of Vip1 pore receptor. It seems too early to consider
potential use of Vip1/Vip2 system for development therapeutic or delivering proteins to specific cellular targets without
further knowledge about receptor binding and pore formation mechanism.
3. And lastly, it is important to complete the nonspecific GFP delivery experiments with negative control when cells are
treated with Vip2-GFP or Vip2NTD-GFP only. Surprising translocation of relatively large folded protein (GFP) through pore
with an inner diameter of 6.0 Å seems inconsistent with Vip1 structure presented in tne same manuscript and requires further
checks and validation.

Response: Thank you for raising this important point. Applying C7 symmetry to Vip1 was
guided by both structural precedent and our own experimental data. Nearly all heptameric
pore-forming components of binary toxins solved by cryo-EM-such as PDB entries 3J9C,
6KLX, 6O2N, 9UE9, 6RB9, and 5JZT-have been refined using the corresponding cyclic
symmetry (see attached table), reflecting the well-established sevenfold architecture of this
protein family. Consistently, our survey of pore-forming toxins in the PDB shows that single-
component heptameric pores are almost universally reconstructed with symmetry imposed,
as this improves resolution without obscuring biologically relevant features.
In our own processing pipeline, we initially refined the Vip1 heptamer in C1, which
yielded a map at ~3.8 Å resolution. When C7 symmetry was applied, the resolution
improved to ~3.3 Å. Importantly, we did not observe evidence of pseudosymmetry or
asymmetry that would be lost upon symmetry imposition. The use of C7 was therefore
motivated primarily by the substantial gain in resolution and the apparent structural
homogeneity of Vip1 alone.

with C7 symmetry and the Vip1-Vip2 complex refined in C1 is not strictly justified, as
symmetry imposition may mask or average out subtle asymmetric features. Accordingly,
we have revised the manuscript to avoid such comparisons.
Instead, we now focus on an internal comparison among the seven Vip1 protomers
within the asymmetric Vip1-Vip2 complex. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 7c-e, six of the
seven Vip1 subunits adopt highly similar conformations, whereas H493 in chain D displays
a distinct conformation relative to the other subunit. This observation supports our original
conclusion that Vip2 binding induces localized conformational differences in Vip1, while
avoiding cross-symmetry comparisons.

Response: Thanks for your insightful comment. We agree that many binary toxins share
similar overall architectures, which is why they are classified within the same toxin family,
much like many GPCRs which can be structurally conserved yet functionally diverse.
However, sequence alignment analyses reveal that Vip1/Vip2 shares ~30% sequence
identity with other well-characterized binary toxins (such as PA/EF/LF, CDTa/b, and Ia/b),
indicating substantial divergence at the primary sequence level.
Importantly, the Vip1/Vip2 binary toxin exhibits behavior markedly differently from
previously characterized binary toxins. While most known binary toxins target humans or
mammals, Vip1/Vip2 is insect-specific, raising a fundamental question: how do binary
toxins with similar overall folds but low sequence identity give rise to such divergent
biological specificities and disease outcomes?
Our structural analysis directly addresses this question. Notably, the regions critical
for Vip2 translocation, including the DTH loop and β-barrel stem, exhibit substantial
sequence divergence (Supplementary Fig.17). As a result, the precise functional roles of
these elements could not be reliably inferred from homology models and required direct
structural determination of the Vip1-Vip2 complex.
Indeed, solving the Vip1-Vip2 complex structure has yielded several novel
mechanistic insights. First, we captured the highest-resolution structural view to date of a
translocation intermediate state among binary toxins, providing an unprecedented
structural snapshot of N-terminal conformational rearrangements during translocation (Fig
3j). Second, we identified the KGF loop as a key structural determinant for specific
recognition and translocation, a role not previously recognized in homologous systems.
Third, analysis of the hydrophobicity profile within the lumen of the β-barrel stem provides
direct evidence supporting a translocation mechanism governed by a hydrophilic pore
environment rather than strict sequence specificity. Fourth, we captured and solved the
structure of the 1:5 (Vip2:Vip1) intermediate complex, revealing an interface between Vip2
and Vip1 that differs from that observed in the heptameric assembly, thereby providing
direct structural evidence for a putative assembly process of Vip2-bound Vip1 oligomers.
Finally, functional assays examining the subcellular localization of the Vip2NTD-GFP fusion
protein provide evidence for the translocation mechanism that is sequence-independent
but lumen hydrophilicity dependent (Fig 5d-e), and highlighting the potential of this system
for protein delivery.
Together, these findings substantially advance our understanding of binary toxin
function and highlight the necessity of obtaining the Vip1-Vip2 complex structure to uncover
system-specific mechanistic features that cannot be inferred from existing binary toxin
structures alone.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment and agree that Bacillus
anthracis protective antigen (PA) represents an important and well-established precedent
for binary toxin–mediated protein delivery. Our study does not aim to claim novelty for the
general concept of toxin-based delivery, but rather to define the distinct biological context
and mechanistic features of the Vip1/Vip2 system.
Unlike PA-mediated delivery, the Vip1/Vip2 toxin functions in the highly alkaline
insect midgut, an environment characterized by markedly different pH, protease
composition, and receptor usage. Our work specifically addresses how the Vip1-Vip2
complex assembles, remains stable, and mediates protein translocation under these
alkaline conditions, which have not been examined in PA-based systems.
At the molecular level, Vip1/Vip2 differs substantially from PA/LF. Vip2 shares only
~17% sequence identity with LF and lacks recognizable PA-binding motifs, making direct
mechanistic extrapolation from PA unreliable. Consistent with this, we show that Vip1-
mediated translocation is hydrophilicity-dependent but sequence-independent, supported
by structural analysis of a predominantly hydrophilic transmembrane pore and by
mutational disruption of pore polarity that abolishes insecticidal activity. We further
demonstrate efficient delivery of both full-length Vip2-GFP and minimal N-terminal fusion
constructs, indicating a level of cargo tolerance specific to this system.
Finally, while PA has been extensively developed as a mammalian delivery
platform, our objective is to establish Vip1/Vip2 as an insect-adapted protein delivery
system with potential applications in precision pest control. We therefore believe that the
novelty of this work lies in revealing how a distinct binary toxin system achieves protein
delivery under insect-specific physiological constraints, rather than in the general principle
of binary toxin-mediated translocation.

representative bacterial pore-forming toxins-including α-hemolysin, anthrax protective

forming toxins, Vip1 shares approximately 30% sequence identity with the binary toxins
PA, Ib, and CDTb (Supplementary Fig. 16a-b). Despite this low sequence identity, the

Supplementary Fig. 16: Sequence identity and structural similarity between Vip1 and other

While discussing translocation mechanism, we also suggest including speculations on
driving forces for substrate protein translocation: differences of proton concentration or
electrical potential across the ϕ-clamp. The former requires protonation-dependent
conformational changes of two or more alternating gates and protonation-dependent
conformational change in ϕ-clamp region. Alternatively, translocation could follow charge-

(PMF), which consists of a proton gradient (ΔpH) and membrane potential (ΔΨ) 22,36-39. A
ΔpH-driven Brownian ratchet mechanism has been proposed, wherein protonation and
deprotonation of acidic residues on the translocating polypeptide facilitate directional

validation, they exceed our current experimental conditions; nonetheless, we now explicitly
acknowledge this as an important direction for future work.
2. Authors also described multiple incomplete assemblies of Vip2-bound Vip-pore
heptamer complex after treatment with high pH (pH 10.4): two-subunit partial pore,1:3

relevance’ of these findings in Discussion section but nonetheless propose a step-wise
assembly pathway based on these ‘intermediate’ structures. No high pH treatment step

earlier, neither for subcellular localization experiments with insect cells reported in this
manuscript. To enable mechanistic understanding of Vip1/Vip1 complex formation and
action, further in vitro experiments are required using model liposomes and Vip2/Vip1 (or
Vip2-GFP/Vip1): Vip2/Vip1 assemblies on liposomes could be treated with high pH and
then used for cryo-EM sample preparation. Image processing of these cryo-EM data would

nature of Vip1 pore receptor. It seems too early to consider potential use of Vip1/Vip2

further knowledge about receptor binding and pore formation mechanism.

particularly the data obtained under high-pH conditions-is insufficient to establish a
stepwise assembly pathway or to support immediate therapeutic applications. In the
revised manuscript, we have explicitly clarified that these assemblies likely represent in
vitro snapshots whose physiological relevance remains uncertain.

resulting incompatibility with vitrification-based cryo-EM sample preparation. As a result,

performed under distinct conditions. Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) detected distinct

transient intermediates under activation conditions. Together, these data indicate
stoichiometric heterogeneity that may reflect progressive stages of assembly, while not
allowing us to specify the exact sequence of events.
To avoid overstating these findings, we have tempered our interpretation
throughout the manuscript. The revised text now states that the observed assemblies
“represent possible intermediate states” rather than establishing a stepwise pathway. While
the identity of the native receptor for Vip1 remains unknown, our data provide a foundation
for future mechanistic studies, including receptor identification and engineering Vip2 for a
more potent bioinsecticide.
Supplementary Fig. 9: Ultracentrifugation analysis of the oligomerization of Vip1 and Vip2.

mediated cross-linking between Vip1 protoxin and His-Vip2-Strep (His-tag at the N-terminus,

monomer), 2′ (Vip2 dimer), α (Vip2 bound to Vip1), β (Vip2 bound to Vip1 oligomers with
varying stoichiometric ratios). The representative blot from three independent assay was shown here.
3. And lastly, it is important to complete the nonspecific GFP delivery experiments with
negative control when cells are treated with Vip2-GFP or Vip2NTD-GFP only. Surprising
translocation of relatively large folded protein (GFP) through pore with an inner diameter
of 6.0 Å seems inconsistent with Vip1 structure presented in tne same manuscript and

Response: Guided by your valuable advices, the negative control and a loss-of-function
triple mutant (E327A/H329A/E370V) were included for the nonspecific GFP delivery
experiments, which further support the nonspecific delivery.
We agree that the reported translocation of folded GFP pore with an inner diameter
of 6.0 Å seems inconsistent with Vip1 structure. To clarify, similar to Vip2, GFP is not
expected to cross the pore in its native folded state. Instead, based on the dynamic
translocation events captured in our study that GFP translocation does not occur in a fully
folded state. Instead, based on the dynamic translocation process we captured (Fig 5,
movie 2), Vip2 undergoes a stepwise partially unfold prior to translocation and passes
through the ϕ-clamp as an extended linear polypeptide chain, which could be then refolded
in the cytosol with assistance from as assisted by chaperon such as Hsp70/90 (Fig 6, DOI:
10.1098/rsob.200089, DOI: 10.1038/nrm.2017.20, DOI: 10.1155/2012/745962).
Furthermore, recent work by Vera et al. has demonstrated the feasibility of a protein-based
anti-CRISPR delivery platform (LF -Acr/PA; DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2426960122), illustrating
that binary toxin systems are capable of delivering fusion proteins, consistent with our
observations. Nonetheless, we agree that further validation will be valuable for
understanding the precise determinants governing GFP translocation.

The authors addressed my concerns, and I recommend the article for publication.

The revised manuscript addresses many questions and concerns raised by the reviewers

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.
